summary: Explains how clients should navigate a Whois++ mesh, where each server refers the client onward to the next appropriate servers. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Whois++ keeps one directory spread across many servers, and each server can point a client at other servers to try next. RFC 1914 writes down how the client should work through that mesh: it asks one server, follows the pointers in the reply, and remembers every server it has already asked so it never goes round in circles.

questions: how to query a whois++ mesh
how do whois++ clients navigate the mesh
what is the directory of servers in whois++
how do whois++ clients detect loops
when should a whois++ client expand a search
subtitle: How a client walks a mesh of Whois++ directory servers without going round in circles.

tldr.problem: A Whois++ mesh spreads one directory across many servers, so a client that finds nothing at its first server has to decide which other servers to ask next.
tldr.mechanism: The client drives the search: it queries one server, follows the servers-to-ask pointers in the reply, and keeps a list of the servers it has already asked so it never asks one twice.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1914 turned mesh traversal into a written-down client algorithm with loop detection, caching and cost limits. It is Historic, so the Whois++ service it describes is no longer part of the current standards.

today: RFC 1914 is Historic, so the Whois++ mesh it describes is not part of the current protocol standards. The unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it, and the document was published in February 1996 as a Standards Track protocol.

sections.title: Overview and Basic Exchange
sections.content:
In the Whois++ architecture, mesh traversal is done by the client, because each server refers the client to the next appropriate server or servers. The exchange itself is simple: the client opens a connection to a server, sends a query, receives a reply, closes the connection, and then decides which server to contact next, if any.

Because the client makes every step of the decision, it needs a written algorithm. The RFC states three goals for that algorithm: referral loops must be detected, cost must be minimised, and the appropriate servers must be contacted rapidly and effectively.

Each client is configured to send queries automatically to one specific Whois++ server. That default server can vary with the template wanted and with the client's place in the index mesh, but the rule is that it should be as local as possible. After a reply arrives, the client has two things it can do. If the number of hits is greater than zero, the response is presented to the user. If the client receives one or many servers-to-ask answers, it should be able to resolve these pointers automatically, which means querying those servers in turn.
sections.plainLanguage: Whois++ keeps one directory spread across many servers. Each server tells the client which other servers to try, so the client, not the servers, decides where to go next. RFC 1914 sets out the rules the client follows so it avoids going round in circles and keeps the search affordable.

sections.title: Expanding a Search
sections.content:
When a query returns no hits, or when the user asks to widen the search, the client should issue a polled-by and a polled-for query to the server it is talking to. The reply names other servers in the mesh, and the client repeats the original query to those servers.

The client must always keep track of which servers it has queried, because it has to detect loops itself by never querying the same server more than once. The RFC puts loop detection in the client rather than in the servers, because it is hard to build into a mesh where each server may take part in several hierarchies at once. Because expansion reaches larger and more comprehensive index servers, the forward knowledge held in the mesh lets the client prune those larger trees quickly.

Blind expansion, however, grows the cost of the search exponentially, and some parts of the mesh charge for responses, so the RFC does not recommend automatic expansion. More sophisticated clients can hold a blacklist of servers to cut off. A server's location does not narrow the search either: a query for companies in the USA does not return only records in US states when the USA server has polled a server in Sweden, so the query has to say country=USA explicitly.

The RFC also describes how an organisation can shorten the path to a partner's records. If organisation A often uses organisation B's server, A can create a local index server that holds the centroid for both organisations, so that a client expanding a search for someone at B resolves the query without first finding the top-level servers of the tree that A and B share.
sections.plainLanguage: When the first server has no answer, the client asks that server which other servers hold records of the same kind, then repeats the original query to each of them. The client remembers what it has already asked so it never asks the same server twice. The RFC warns that widening a search this way can get expensive, so a client should be able to stop and to block servers it does not want to contact.

sections.title: The Client Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC gives the algorithm as a list of steps over four working variables: Query, the data to search for; QueriedServers, the servers already contacted; AnswerList, the answers gathered so far; and OriginalServers, the servers known to the client.

The outer loop runs while there are servers to work through. The inner loop takes the first server on the list, and if that server is not in QueriedServers, sends it the query, adds the servers it refers to as servers-to-ask, and appends the answers to AnswerList. When the list empties and the query should be expanded, the client sends a polled-for query to each server it has contacted and puts the replies into a fresh set of original servers for the next pass. At the end it displays AnswerList to the user.

Following this algorithm finds all the records in the mesh that the first Whois++ server queried belongs to. The worked example in the RFC shows that it still works when the mesh is not a tree, because a server such as the Swedish branch of a multinational company can be polled both by the national server in Sweden and by the head-office server in the United States.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the client's steps in order. It keeps a list of servers it has asked, a list of servers it still has to ask, and a list of answers collected so far. It works through the list, skips any server already asked, and after each pass asks every contacted server which other servers it knows about. When nothing is left, it shows the collected answers.

sections.title: The Directory of Servers
sections.content:
The second way to find the right server is a separate service, the Directory of Servers. It is a special Whois++ server that polls every other Whois++ server for information about the records that server holds.

The client uses it in two steps. The hostname and port number of the Directory of Servers have to be preconfigured in this version of the protocol. The client then queries it for serverhandle records, for example for country sweden, which returns information on all the servers that serve that template and country. Presenting that list to the user lets the search start at a closer server.

Every serverhandle record must carry the server's Server-Handle, its current Host-Name and its current Host-Port. A record may also carry contact and descriptive attributes such as Admin-Name, Admin-Email, Admin-Phone, Organization-Name, Description, Menu-Item, City, State and Country, plus any other attribute that identifies the records on that server. The RFC says this information is meant to be shown to a user, and it does not think the selection should be automatic in the client. A future technique might make the choice automatic, depending on the query the user issues.
sections.plainLanguage: One special server keeps a list of the other servers and what each one holds. A client asks it which servers deal with a particular template and country, and shows that list so the user can begin closer to the answer. The RFC says this choice should stay with the user for now.

sections.title: Caching and Cost Control
sections.content:
A client can cache everything it gets from a server, for example records, the IP addresses of Whois++ servers and the address of the Directory of Servers, and it chooses for how long to hold each item. The IP address of the Directory of Servers might not change for a day or two, and neither might other information.

The hostname, IP address and port number returned in a servers-to-ask reply are the values cached at the server's last poll, which might have been several weeks earlier. When such a connection fails, the client should fall back on the server handle: it contacts the Directory of Servers, asks for the server with that handle, and gets the last known hostname before retrying.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can keep the records, addresses and server details it has already received instead of asking again. Because a referral can name a hostname that is weeks old, a failed connection sends the client back to the Directory of Servers, which supplies the current hostname for that server.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC refers the reader to the Whois++ architecture document for the security considerations of the protocol itself. What it adds here is about the client. A client should be able to hold a blacklist of servers it must not query, because fake Whois++ servers can be put up on the network; once such a server is found, the user should be able to configure the client never to query it.

The RFC also asks the client to be careful when expanding a query, whether by normal expansion or through the Directory of Servers. A query can take a long time, so the user should be able to quit in the middle of such a transaction. The RFC describes this as a question of user interaction more than a plain security issue.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC leaves the security of the service to another document and concentrates on what the client must be able to do. It must be able to block a server that turns out to be fake, and it must be able to abandon a long-running search at the user's request.
